notes.h: Signals: classification, energy, power and elementary functions
notes.body:
A signal is a function carrying information: continuous-time x(t), or discrete-time x[n] defined only at integer n.

Classifications:
- Periodic: x(t + T) = x(t) for all t. The fundamental period T0 is the smallest such T, and ω0 = 2π/T0. A sum of sinusoids is periodic only if the ratio of their periods is rational; the fundamental period is then the least common multiple of the individual periods.
- Discrete sinusoids: cos(Ω0 n) is periodic only if Ω0/(2π) is rational. So cos(πn/4) has period N = 8, but cos(n) is not periodic at all.
- Even and odd: any signal splits into xe(t) = ½[x(t) + x(−t)] and xo(t) = ½[x(t) − x(−t)].

Energy and power (normalised to a 1 Ω resistor):
- Energy: E = ∫|x(t)|² dt over all t.
- Average power: P = lim (1/2T)∫ from −T to T of |x(t)|² dt.
- An energy signal has finite E, so P = 0. A power signal has finite non-zero P, so E is infinite. Some signals, such as e^t, are neither.
- A sinusoid A cos(ωt + φ) has P = A²/2. For a sum of sinusoids at distinct frequencies, the powers add.

Elementary signals:
- Unit step u(t): 0 for t < 0 and 1 for t > 0.
- Unit impulse δ(t): zero except at t = 0, with unit area; δ(t) = du/dt.
- Sifting property: ∫x(t)δ(t − t0) dt = x(t0). Also x(t)δ(t − t0) = x(t0)δ(t − t0).
- Ramp r(t) = t·u(t), and the complex exponential e^(st) with s = σ + jω.

Transformations of the independent variable: in x(at − b), shift first and then scale. Rewrite it as x(a(t − b/a)): the signal is compressed by a factor a and shifted right by b/a. In discrete time, decimation x[2n] discards samples.

Worked example: x(t) = e^(−2t)u(t) has E = ∫ from 0 to ∞ of e^(−4t) dt = 1/4 J (normalised), so it is an energy signal. By contrast x(t) = 3 cos(100πt) has P = 9/2 = 4.5 W and infinite energy, so it is a power signal. The sum cos(2t) + cos(3t) has periods π and 2π/3. Their ratio is 3/2, which is rational, so the sum is periodic with T0 = 2π.

Exam pitfalls:
- Scaling by a and then shifting by b instead of b/a. If you scale first, the shift must be divided by a.
- Assuming every discrete sinusoid is periodic.
- Adding the powers of two sinusoids at the same frequency. Their phases matter, so combine them first.
- Treating δ(t) as an ordinary function with value 1 at t = 0. Only its area is defined.

notes.h: LTI systems, impulse response and convolution
notes.body:
A system maps an input signal to an output. Key properties:
- Linear: superposition holds. If x1 → y1 and x2 → y2, then ax1 + bx2 → ay1 + by2. A useful test: zero input must give zero output.
- Time-invariant: a delayed input gives an equally delayed output. Coefficients that depend explicitly on t, as in y(t) = t·x(t), break time invariance.
- Causal: the output depends only on present and past inputs. y(t) = x(t + 1) is not causal.
- Memoryless: depends only on the present input.
- BIBO stable: every bounded input gives a bounded output.

For a linear time-invariant (LTI) system, the impulse response h(t) fully characterises the system. Any input can be written as a weighted sum of shifted impulses, so the output is the convolution:
y(t) = (x * h)(t) = ∫x(τ)h(t − τ) dτ
In discrete time, y[n] = Σ x[k]h[n − k].

Properties of convolution: it is commutative, associative (so cascaded systems combine to h1 * h2) and distributive (so parallel systems combine to h1 + h2). Convolving with δ(t − t0) delays a signal by t0.

LTI properties from h:
- Causal if and only if h(t) = 0 for t < 0.
- BIBO stable if and only if ∫|h(t)| dt is finite (Σ|h[n]| for discrete time).
- The step response is the running integral of h(t). Equivalently, h(t) is the derivative of the step response.

Graphical method ("flip and slide"): flip h(τ) to get h(−τ), shift it by t, multiply by x(τ) and integrate the overlap. Work through each range of t in which the overlap changes form.

Discrete example: [1, 2, 1] * [1, 1] = [1, 3, 3, 1]. The output length is 3 + 2 − 1 = 4 samples.

Worked example: x(t) = u(t) and h(t) = e^(−t)u(t), which is an RC low-pass filter with τ = 1 s. For t > 0, y(t) = ∫ from 0 to t of e^(−(t−τ)) dτ = 1 − e^(−t). This is the familiar capacitor-charging curve. The system is stable because ∫|h| dt = 1.

Eigenfunctions: e^(st) passes through any LTI system unchanged in shape: e^(st) → H(s)e^(st). This is why Laplace and Fourier methods work, and why a sinusoid in gives a sinusoid out at the same frequency.

Exam pitfalls:
- Forgetting to flip h before sliding (this matters unless h is symmetric).
- Wrong integration limits. Find where both functions are non-zero for each range of t.
- Calling y = 2x + 3 linear. It is affine, and fails the zero-in, zero-out test.
- Testing BIBO stability with one particular input rather than proving it for every bounded input.

The (unilateral) Laplace transform is F(s) = ∫ from 0⁻ to ∞ of f(t)e^(−st) dt, with s = σ + jω. It turns linear constant-coefficient differential equations into algebraic equations, and builds initial conditions in automatically.

Key pairs:
- δ(t) → 1
- u(t) → 1/s
- t·u(t) → 1/s²
- e^(−at)u(t) → 1/(s + a)
- sin ωt → ω/(s² + ω²) and cos ωt → s/(s² + ω²)
- e^(−at)sin ωt → ω/((s + a)² + ω²)

Key properties:
- Differentiation: f′(t) → sF(s) − f(0⁻), and f″(t) → s²F(s) − s·f(0⁻) − f′(0⁻).
- Integration: divides by s.
- Time delay: f(t − T)u(t − T) → e^(−sT)F(s).
- Frequency shift: e^(−at)f(t) → F(s + a).
- Convolution in time becomes multiplication: x * h → X(s)H(s).
- Final value theorem: f(∞) = lim as s → 0 of sF(s). It is valid only if sF(s) has all its poles in the open left half-plane.
- Initial value theorem: f(0⁺) = lim as s → ∞ of sF(s).

Transfer function: H(s) = Y(s)/X(s) with zero initial conditions. It is the Laplace transform of the impulse response. Roots of the numerator are zeros and roots of the denominator are poles. Poles fix the natural modes: a real pole at −a gives e^(−at), and a complex pair −σ ± jωd gives e^(−σt)sin(ωd t + φ).

Standard second-order form: H(s) = K ωn²/(s² + 2ζωn s + ωn²), with poles at −ζωn ± jωn√(1 − ζ²).

Inverse transforms use partial fractions. For distinct poles, the residue at s = p is [(s − p)F(s)] evaluated at s = p (cover-up rule). Repeated poles need terms in 1/(s − p)², and so on. Complex pairs are best handled by completing the square.

Worked example: y″ + 3y′ + 2y = 3u(t) with zero initial conditions.
- Transform: (s² + 3s + 2)Y = 3/s, so Y = 3/(s(s + 1)(s + 2)).
- Residues: at s = 0, 3/2; at s = −1, 3/((−1)(1)) = −3; at s = −2, 3/((−2)(−1)) = 3/2.
- So y(t) = 1.5 − 3e^(−t) + 1.5e^(−2t). Check: y(0) = 0, and the final value theorem gives 3/2.

Block diagrams: blocks in series multiply, blocks in parallel add, and a negative-feedback loop reduces to G/(1 + GH).

Exam pitfalls:
- Using the final value theorem on an unstable or oscillatory system. It gives a meaningless answer.
- Dropping initial-condition terms in the derivative property.
- Sign errors in residues when using the cover-up rule.
- Confusing the transfer function (zero initial conditions) with the full solution.

For a stable LTI system with transfer function H(s), the steady-state response to A cos(ωt + φ) is A|H(jω)| cos(ωt + φ + ∠H(jω)). The frequency response H(jω) is H(s) evaluated on the imaginary axis. Its magnitude scales each frequency and its phase shifts it.

Decibels: gain in dB = 20 log₁₀|H|, so ×10 is +20 dB, ×2 is about +6 dB and 1/√2 is −3 dB. Cascaded blocks add in dB, and their phases add.

Asymptotic Bode rules, writing each factor in time-constant form (1 + s/ωc):
- Constant K: flat line at 20 log₁₀ K with 0° phase (or −180° if K < 0).
- Pole at the origin, 1/s: −20 dB/decade passing through 0 dB at ω = 1, with −90° phase.
- Real pole 1/(1 + s/ωc): flat, then −20 dB/decade above the corner ωc. The true curve is −3 dB at the corner. The phase falls from 0 to −90°, passing −45° at ωc, and the change happens mostly between 0.1ωc and 10ωc.
- Real zero: the mirror image, with +20 dB/decade and phase rising to +90°.
- Second-order pole pair: −40 dB/decade above ωn, phase from 0 to −180° (−90° at ωn). When ζ < 1/√2 there is a resonant peak Mr = 1/(2ζ√(1 − ζ²)) at ωr = ωn√(1 − 2ζ²).

Filters: a first-order RC low-pass has H = 1/(1 + jωRC) and fc = 1/(2πRC). An nth-order Butterworth filter is maximally flat and rolls off at 20n dB/decade.

Bandwidth is usually where the gain falls 3 dB below its low-frequency value. Faster systems need more bandwidth.

Minimum-phase systems have all poles and zeros in the left half-plane. For them, magnitude and phase are linked, so a slope of −20n dB/decade corresponds roughly to −90n° phase. A right-half-plane zero has the same magnitude curve as its left-half-plane mirror image but adds phase lag instead of lead. A time delay e^(−sT) has unit magnitude and adds phase lag ωT. Both add lag that the magnitude plot does not reveal.

Worked example: H(s) = 100/(s + 10) = 10/(1 + s/10).
- The DC gain is 10, which is 20 dB, and the corner is at 10 rad/s.
- At ω = 10: |H| = 100/|10 + 10j| = 7.07, which is 17.0 dB (3 dB below 20 dB), and the phase is −45°.
- At ω = 100 the asymptote gives 0 dB. The exact value is 20 log₁₀(100/100.5) = −0.04 dB, with phase −84.3°.

Exam pitfalls:
- Writing poles as (s + a) instead of normalising to a(1 + s/a). The DC gain is then misplaced.
- Using 10 log₁₀ for voltage gain. It should be 20 log₁₀; 10 log₁₀ is for power ratios.
- Forgetting the −3 dB correction at a corner, or the resonant peak for low ζ.
- Mixing hertz and rad/s.

notes.h: Feedback control: closed-loop behaviour and steady-state error
notes.body:
In a negative-feedback loop, a controller C(s) drives a plant G(s) and a sensor H(s) measures the output. The loop gain is L(s) = C(s)G(s)H(s). With unity feedback (H = 1):
- Closed-loop transfer function: T(s) = Y/R = CG/(1 + CG).
- Sensitivity: S(s) = 1/(1 + L), with S + T = 1.

Why use feedback:
- Reduced sensitivity to plant variation: dT/T = S·dG/G, so where |L| is large, plant changes have little effect.
- Disturbance rejection: an output disturbance is multiplied by S.
- It can stabilise an unstable plant and speed up its response.
The costs are measurement noise feeding into the output (it is multiplied by T), the risk of instability, and the need for a good sensor.

Second-order specifications, for T(s) = ωn²/(s² + 2ζωn s + ωn²) with 0 < ζ < 1:
- Percentage overshoot: e^(−ζπ/√(1 − ζ²)) × 100%. ζ = 0.5 gives 16.3% and ζ = 0.7 gives 4.6%.
- Peak time: tp = π/(ωn√(1 − ζ²)).
- 2% settling time: ts ≈ 4/(ζωn).
- 10–90% rise time: about 1.8/ωn when ζ is near 0.5 (an approximation).
Higher-order systems are often approximated by their dominant (slowest) poles.

Steady-state error (unity feedback, stable closed loop): e(∞) = lim as s → 0 of sR(s)/(1 + L(s)). The system type is the number of pure integrators (poles at s = 0) in L(s).
- Step input: e = 1/(1 + Kp), where Kp = L(0). Type 0 gives a finite error; type 1 or above gives zero.
- Ramp input: e = 1/Kv, where Kv = lim sL(s). Type 1 gives a finite error.
- Parabolic input: e = 1/Ka, where Ka = lim s²L(s).

Worked example: L(s) = K/(s(s + 4)) with K = 16.
- T = 16/(s² + 4s + 16), so ωn = 4 rad/s and ζ = 4/(2 × 4) = 0.5.
- Overshoot 16.3%, tp = π/(4 × 0.866) = 0.91 s and ts ≈ 4/2 = 2 s.
- Type 1, so the step error is zero. Kv = 16/4 = 4, so a unit ramp leaves an error of 0.25.
- Raising K to 64 cuts the ramp error to 0.0625, but ζ drops to 0.25 and overshoot rises to 44%. This trade-off is what motivates compensators.

Exam pitfalls:
- Applying the error formulas without first checking closed-loop stability.
- Using Kp for a ramp input, or counting integrators in the controller and the plant separately when the type depends on the whole loop.
- Forgetting that ts depends only on the real part of the poles (ζωn).
- Assuming that higher gain always helps.

notes.h: Stability: poles, Routh–Hurwitz and stability margins
notes.body:
An LTI system is BIBO stable if and only if every pole of its transfer function (after any cancellations) lies strictly in the left half of the s-plane. Simple imaginary-axis poles give marginal stability (sustained oscillation); right-half-plane or repeated imaginary-axis poles mean instability. In discrete time the stability boundary is the unit circle in the z-plane.

For a feedback loop, the closed-loop poles are the roots of 1 + L(s) = 0; the root locus plots how they move with gain.

Routh–Hurwitz criterion: it tests stability without solving for the roots.
- Necessary condition: all coefficients of the characteristic polynomial are present and have the same sign.
- Build the Routh array from the coefficients. The number of sign changes in the first column equals the number of right-half-plane roots.
- Special cases: a zero in the first column (replace it by a small ε), or a whole row of zeros. A zero row signals roots symmetric about the origin; the auxiliary polynomial from the row above gives them.

Worked example: L(s) = K/(s(s + 1)(s + 5)) gives the characteristic equation s³ + 6s² + 5s + K = 0.
- Routh array: s³: 1, 5. s²: 6, K. s¹: (30 − K)/6. s⁰: K.
- Stability needs 0 < K < 30.
- At K = 30 the auxiliary equation 6s² + 30 = 0 gives s = ±j√5, so the loop oscillates at √5 = 2.24 rad/s.

Frequency-domain margins, read from Bode plots of L(jω):
- Gain margin (GM): the factor by which the gain can rise before instability, measured at the phase-crossover frequency where ∠L = −180°. GM = 1/|L|, or −20 log₁₀|L| in dB.
- Phase margin (PM): 180° + ∠L at the gain-crossover frequency where |L| = 1.
- Typical targets are GM ≥ 6 dB and PM of 30–60°. A rule of thumb is ζ ≈ PM/100 for PM up to about 60°.
In the example, K = 10 gives GM = 30/10 = 3, or 9.5 dB. The gain crossover is at about 1.23 rad/s with PM ≈ 25°.

Nyquist criterion: Z = N + P, where P is the number of open-loop right-half-plane poles and N is the number of clockwise encirclements of −1 by the Nyquist plot of L(jω). The closed loop is stable when Z = 0. An open-loop unstable plant therefore needs anticlockwise encirclements of −1.

Exam pitfalls:
- Concluding stability from the coefficient signs alone. That condition is sufficient only for first- and second-order polynomials.
- Misreading the margins of a conditionally stable system, where reducing the gain can also cause instability.
- Ignoring the phase lag added by time delay.

notes.h: PID control: actions, tuning and practical issues
notes.body:
A PID controller acts on the error e = r − y:
u(t) = Kp e + Ki ∫e dt + Kd de/dt
so C(s) = Kp + Ki/s + Kd·s. In the "standard" form this is Kp(1 + 1/(Ti s) + Td s), with Ki = Kp/Ti and Kd = Kp·Td.

Effect of each term:
- Proportional: a larger Kp gives a faster response and a smaller (but non-zero) steady-state error for a type-0 plant. It usually increases overshoot and reduces stability margins.
- Integral: adds a pole at the origin, which raises the system type and removes steady-state error to steps and step disturbances. It adds phase lag (−90° at low frequency), which tends to increase overshoot and slow settling. It causes integrator windup when the actuator saturates.
- Derivative: anticipates error by reacting to its rate of change. It adds phase lead and damping, reducing overshoot. It amplifies high-frequency noise, so practical controllers filter it: Kd·s/(1 + sTf), with Tf typically a small fraction of Td.

Practical refinements:
- Anti-windup: stop integrating, or back-calculate, while the actuator is saturated.
- Derivative on measurement: use −dy/dt instead of de/dt, which avoids a "derivative kick" when the setpoint steps.
- Setpoint weighting, and bumpless transfer between manual and automatic modes.

Ziegler–Nichols ultimate-gain tuning (1942): with integral and derivative action off, raise Kp until the loop oscillates steadily at gain Ku and period Pu. Then:
- P only: Kp = 0.5Ku.
- PI: Kp = 0.45Ku, Ti = Pu/1.2.
- PID: Kp = 0.6Ku, Ti = Pu/2, Td = Pu/8.
These target quarter-amplitude decay, which is aggressive, so the gains are commonly detuned afterwards. Model-based alternatives include IMC/lambda tuning and loop shaping.

Worked example: for L(s) = K/(s(s + 1)(s + 5)), Routh analysis gave Ku = 30 and an oscillation at ω = √5 rad/s, so Pu = 2π/√5 = 2.81 s. The Ziegler–Nichols PID settings are:
- Kp = 18, Ti = 1.40 s, Td = 0.351 s.
- Hence Ki = 18/1.40 = 12.8 s⁻¹ and Kd = 18 × 0.351 = 6.32 s.
The plant already contains an integrator, so a P or PD controller already gives zero steady-state error to setpoint steps. The integral term is needed to reject constant load disturbances entering before the integrator.

PI with pole–zero cancellation: for a first-order plant K/(τs + 1), choosing Ti = τ makes the loop gain KKp/(τs). The closed loop is then first order with time constant τ/(KKp).

Exam pitfalls:
- Claiming integral action always helps: it removes offset but costs phase margin.
- Confusing parallel gains (Ki, Kd) with standard-form times (Ti, Td).
- Forgetting actuator limits.

Fourier series: a periodic signal with period T0 (ω0 = 2π/T0) that satisfies the Dirichlet conditions can be written as
x(t) = a0 + Σ [an cos(nω0t) + bn sin(nω0t)]
The coefficients are a0 = (1/T0)∫x dt, an = (2/T0)∫x cos(nω0t) dt and bn = (2/T0)∫x sin(nω0t) dt. The exponential form is x(t) = Σ cn e^(jnω0t).
- Even signals have only cosine terms; odd signals have only sine terms.
- Half-wave symmetry, x(t + T0/2) = −x(t), means only odd harmonics are present.

Example: a square wave switching between ±A, written as an odd function, has the series (4A/π)[sin ω0t + (1/3)sin 3ω0t + (1/5)sin 5ω0t + ...]. The fundamental carries (4A/π)²/2 ÷ A² = 8/π² ≈ 81% of the total power. Near each jump the partial sums overshoot by about 9% of the jump size however many terms are used. This is the Gibbs phenomenon.

Parseval's theorem: average power = Σ|cn|². Power is shared out among the harmonics.

Fourier transform for aperiodic signals: X(ω) = ∫x(t)e^(−jωt) dt.
- A rectangular pulse transforms to a sinc function.
- e^(−at)u(t) → 1/(a + jω) for a > 0.
- δ(t) → 1.
Convolution in time becomes multiplication in frequency, and shorter pulses have wider spectra.

Sampling: taking x[n] = x(nTs) at rate fs = 1/Ts makes the spectrum repeat at every multiple of fs.
- Nyquist–Shannon theorem: a signal band-limited to fmax can be reconstructed exactly if fs > 2fmax. The quantity 2fmax is the Nyquist rate and fs/2 is the Nyquist frequency.
- Aliasing: a component at f appears at |f − k·fs| for the integer k that brings it into the range 0 to fs/2. Once sampled, aliases cannot be separated from genuine signals. An analogue anti-aliasing low-pass filter must therefore come before the sampler.

Discrete Fourier transform (DFT): X[k] = Σ from n = 0 to N − 1 of x[n]e^(−j2πkn/N). The bin spacing is Δf = fs/N, and bin k corresponds to k·fs/N for k up to N/2. The FFT computes it in O(N log N) operations; windowing reduces spectral leakage.

Worked example: sampling at fs = 8 kHz with N = 256 gives Δf = 31.25 Hz, so a 1 kHz tone lands in bin 32. A 6 kHz tone sampled without a filter aliases to |6 − 8| = 2 kHz and appears in bin 64, indistinguishable from a real 2 kHz signal.

Exam pitfalls:
- Saying fs = 2fmax is sufficient. Strictly fs must exceed 2fmax, and in practice it needs a margin.
- Placing the anti-aliasing filter after the ADC.
- Confusing frequency resolution (fs/N, set by record length) with the highest frequency (fs/2).

cards.f: Define an energy signal and a power signal.
cards.b: An energy signal has finite total energy E = ∫|x|² dt, so its average power is zero. A power signal has finite non-zero average power, so its energy is infinite.

cards.f: What is the average power of A cos(ωt + φ)?
cards.b: P = A²/2 (normalised to 1 Ω), whatever the values of ω and φ.

cards.f: State the sifting property of the unit impulse.
cards.b: ∫x(t)δ(t − t0) dt = x(t0). Integrating against a shifted impulse picks out the value of x at t0.

cards.f: How are the even and odd parts of a signal defined?
cards.b: xe(t) = ½[x(t) + x(−t)] and xo(t) = ½[x(t) − x(−t)]. They sum to x(t).

cards.f: When is a sum of two continuous-time sinusoids periodic?
cards.b: When the ratio of their periods (or frequencies) is a rational number. The fundamental period is then the least common multiple of the two periods.

cards.f: Is x[n] = cos(n) periodic? Explain.
cards.b: No. A discrete sinusoid cos(Ω0 n) is periodic only if Ω0/(2π) is rational, and 1/(2π) is irrational.

cards.f: Find the period of x[n] = cos(πn/4).
cards.b: Ω0/(2π) = 1/8, so the fundamental period is N = 8 samples.

cards.f: Find the energy of x(t) = e^(−2t)u(t).
cards.b: E = ∫ from 0 to ∞ of e^(−4t) dt = 1/4 (normalised units).

cards.f: Describe how to sketch x(2t − 4) from x(t).
cards.b: Write it as x(2(t − 2)): compress x(t) by a factor of 2, then shift it right by 2. The shift is not 4.

cards.f: How are the unit step and unit impulse related?
cards.b: δ(t) = du(t)/dt, and u(t) is the running integral of δ(t).

cards.f: State the conditions for a system to be linear.
cards.b: It must satisfy superposition: ax1 + bx2 produces ay1 + by2 for all inputs and constants. This implies zero input gives zero output.

cards.f: Why is y(t) = t·x(t) not time-invariant?
cards.b: Delaying the input gives t·x(t − T), but delaying the output gives (t − T)x(t − T). These differ, because the gain depends explicitly on time.

cards.f: Write the convolution integral for an LTI system.
cards.b: y(t) = ∫x(τ)h(t − τ) dτ, integrated over all τ. In discrete time, y[n] = Σ x[k]h[n − k].

cards.f: What is the condition on h(t) for an LTI system to be BIBO stable?
cards.b: The impulse response must be absolutely integrable: ∫|h(t)| dt < ∞ (or Σ|h[n]| < ∞ in discrete time).

cards.f: What is the condition on h(t) for an LTI system to be causal?
cards.b: h(t) = 0 for all t < 0.
[1, 1, 1, −3]. The output has 3 + 2 − 1 = 4 samples.

cards.f: How do cascaded and parallel LTI systems combine?
cards.b: Cascaded systems give h1 * h2, which is H1H2 in the transform domain, and the order does not matter. Parallel systems give h1 + h2.

cards.f: Why is e^(st) called an eigenfunction of LTI systems?
cards.b: Passing it through an LTI system returns H(s)e^(st): the same function scaled by a complex constant.

cards.f: Is y = 3x + 2 a linear system?
cards.b: No. It is affine: zero input gives an output of 2, which violates superposition.

cards.f: How are an LTI system's step response and impulse response related?
cards.b: The step response is the running integral of h(t). Equivalently, h(t) is the derivative of the step response.

cards.f: Give the Laplace transforms of u(t), e^(−at)u(t) and t·u(t).
cards.b: They are 1/s, 1/(s + a) and 1/s² respectively.

cards.f: Write the Laplace transform of f′(t) including the initial condition.
State the final value theorem and its condition.
cards.b: f(∞) = lim as s → 0 of sF(s). It is valid only if all poles of sF(s) lie in the open left half-plane.

cards.f: What is a transfer function?
cards.b: The ratio Y(s)/X(s) with all initial conditions zero. It equals the Laplace transform of the impulse response.

cards.f: What time-domain behaviour does a complex pole pair at −σ ± jωd produce?
cards.b: A damped sinusoid proportional to e^(−σt)sin(ωd t + φ).

cards.f: Give the Laplace transform of a delayed signal f(t − T)u(t − T).
cards.b: e^(−sT)F(s).

cards.f: Find the residue of 3/(s(s + 1)(s + 2)) at s = −1.
Where are the poles of ωn²/(s² + 2ζωn s + ωn²) for 0 < ζ < 1?
cards.b: At s = −ζωn ± jωn√(1 − ζ²).

cards.f: Why is the final value theorem invalid for F(s) = 1/(s² + 4)?
cards.b: The poles at ±j2 lie on the imaginary axis, so f(t) = ½ sin 2t oscillates and never settles. The theorem would wrongly give 0.

cards.f: State the initial value theorem.
cards.b: f(0⁺) = lim as s → ∞ of sF(s), provided the limit exists.

cards.f: What is the steady-state output of a stable LTI system driven by A cos(ωt)?
cards.b: A|H(jω)| cos(ωt + ∠H(jω)): the same frequency, with the amplitude scaled and the phase shifted.

cards.f: Convert a voltage gain of 0.1 and a voltage gain of 2 to decibels.
cards.b: 20 log₁₀ 0.1 = −20 dB and 20 log₁₀ 2 ≈ +6.0 dB.

cards.f: Give the asymptotic magnitude slope and the phase at the corner for a single real pole.
cards.b: The slope is −20 dB/decade above the corner. The phase there is −45°, heading towards −90°.

cards.f: How far is the true magnitude below the asymptote at a first-order corner frequency?
Give the corner frequency of an RC low-pass filter.
cards.b: ωc = 1/(RC) rad/s, so fc = 1/(2πRC) Hz.

cards.f: Give the resonant peak magnitude and frequency of a standard second-order system.
cards.b: Mr = 1/(2ζ√(1 − ζ²)) at ωr = ωn√(1 − 2ζ²). This applies only when ζ < 1/√2.

cards.f: What is the high-frequency roll-off of an nth-order Butterworth low-pass filter?
cards.b: 20n dB/decade. The passband is maximally flat and the gain is −3 dB at the cutoff.

cards.f: What does a pure time delay e^(−sT) do to the frequency response?
cards.b: Its magnitude is 1 at all frequencies, so the magnitude response is unchanged. It adds phase lag of ωT radians, which grows without limit as frequency rises.

cards.f: What is a minimum-phase system?
cards.b: One with all its poles and zeros in the left half-plane. Its phase is then determined by its magnitude response.

cards.f: Find |H| and the phase of H(s) = 100/(s + 10) at ω = 10 rad/s.
cards.b: |H| = 100/√200 = 7.07, which is 17.0 dB, and the phase is −45°.

cards.f: Give the closed-loop transfer function of a negative-feedback loop.
cards.b: T(s) = G(s)/(1 + G(s)H(s)), where G is the forward path and H the feedback path.

cards.f: Define the sensitivity function and its relation to T.
cards.b: S = 1/(1 + L), where L is the loop gain. With unity feedback, S + T = 1.

cards.f: Give the percentage overshoot of a second-order step response.
cards.b: %OS = 100 e^(−ζπ/√(1 − ζ²)). For example, ζ = 0.5 gives about 16.3%.

cards.f: Give the peak time and the 2% settling time of a second-order step response.
cards.b: tp = π/(ωn√(1 − ζ²)) and ts ≈ 4/(ζωn).

cards.f: What is the system type of a feedback loop?
cards.b: The number of pure integrators (poles at s = 0) in the open-loop transfer function L(s).

cards.f: Give the steady-state error of a type-0 unity-feedback system to a unit step.
cards.b: e = 1/(1 + Kp), where Kp = L(0) is the position error constant.

cards.f: Give the steady-state error of a type-1 system to a unit ramp.
cards.b: e = 1/Kv, where Kv = lim as s → 0 of s·L(s).

cards.f: How does feedback reduce sensitivity to plant changes?
cards.b: dT/T = S·dG/G. Where |L| is large, S is small, so a plant change produces a much smaller relative change in closed-loop behaviour.

cards.f: For L = K/(s(s + 4)), what K gives ζ = 0.5?
cards.b: The characteristic equation is s² + 4s + K, so 2ζωn = 4 gives ωn = 4 and K = ωn² = 16.

cards.f: Name two costs of using high loop gain.
cards.b: Reduced stability margins (more overshoot, possible instability) and greater transmission of sensor noise. Large actuator demands can also cause saturation.

cards.f: State the pole condition for BIBO stability of a continuous-time LTI system.
cards.b: All poles must lie strictly in the left half of the s-plane (negative real parts).

cards.f: What does the number of sign changes in the first column of a Routh array tell you?
cards.b: It equals the number of roots of the characteristic polynomial in the right half-plane.

cards.f: What does a whole row of zeros in a Routh array indicate?
cards.b: Roots symmetric about the origin, often an imaginary-axis pair. The auxiliary polynomial from the row above gives them.

cards.f: Define gain margin.
cards.b: The factor by which the loop gain can be increased before instability: 1/|L(jω)| at the frequency where ∠L = −180°, often given in dB.

cards.f: Define phase margin.
cards.b: 180° + ∠L(jω) at the gain-crossover frequency where |L| = 1. It is the extra phase lag the loop can tolerate before instability.

cards.f: For s³ + 6s² + 5s + K, find the range of K for stability.
cards.b: The first-column s¹ entry is (30 − K)/6 and the s⁰ entry is K, so stability needs 0 < K < 30.

cards.f: State the Nyquist stability criterion.
cards.b: Z = N + P, where P is the number of open-loop RHP poles and N the number of clockwise encirclements of −1. The closed loop is stable if Z = 0.

cards.f: Is a polynomial with all-positive coefficients necessarily stable?
cards.b: Only for first- and second-order polynomials. From third order upwards the Routh test is needed; for example s³ + s² + s + 2 is unstable.

cards.f: What is a rule of thumb linking phase margin to closed-loop damping?
cards.b: For second-order-like loops, ζ ≈ PM/100 with PM in degrees, up to about 60°. So PM = 45° suggests ζ ≈ 0.45.

cards.f: Why does time delay threaten stability?
cards.b: It adds phase lag ωT without reducing the gain. This lowers the phase margin and can push the loop past −180° at the gain crossover.

cards.f: Write the PID control law in parallel form and standard form.
cards.b: Parallel: C(s) = Kp + Ki/s + Kd·s. Standard: Kp(1 + 1/(Ti s) + Td s), with Ki = Kp/Ti and Kd = Kp·Td.

cards.f: What is the main benefit of integral action?
cards.b: It adds a pole at the origin, raising the system type, so steady-state error to steps and step disturbances is removed.

cards.f: What does derivative action contribute, and what is its main drawback?
cards.b: It adds phase lead and damping, which reduces overshoot. It amplifies high-frequency noise, so it needs a filter.

cards.f: What is integrator windup and how is it prevented?
cards.b: While the actuator is saturated, the integral keeps growing, which causes large overshoot afterwards. It is prevented by clamping the integrator or by back-calculation.

cards.f: What is derivative kick and how is it avoided?
cards.b: A setpoint step makes de/dt very large, producing a spike in the controller output. It is avoided by differentiating the measurement (−dy/dt) instead of the error.

cards.f: Give the Ziegler–Nichols ultimate-gain PID settings.
cards.b: Kp = 0.6Ku, Ti = Pu/2 and Td = Pu/8, where Ku and Pu are the gain and period of sustained oscillation.

cards.f: What response do Ziegler–Nichols settings aim for, and what is the usual consequence?
cards.b: Quarter-amplitude decay. This is quite oscillatory, with large overshoot, so the gains are usually detuned afterwards.

cards.f: Why does proportional-only control leave a steady-state error on a type-0 plant?
cards.b: A non-zero control signal needs a non-zero error. The error settles at 1/(1 + KpG(0)) for a unit step.

cards.f: How can a PI controller's zero be placed to simplify a first-order plant K/(τs + 1)?
cards.b: Set Ti = τ to cancel the plant pole. The loop becomes KKp/(τs), giving a first-order closed loop with time constant τ/(KKp).

cards.f: Why might a PID loop on a plant that already has an integrator still need integral action?
cards.b: To remove the steady-state error caused by constant load disturbances entering before the plant integrator. The plant integrator removes setpoint error only.

cards.f: State the Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem.
cards.b: A signal band-limited to fmax can be reconstructed exactly from samples taken at fs > 2fmax.

cards.f: What is aliasing?
cards.b: Frequencies above fs/2 appear after sampling at a lower apparent frequency |f − k·fs|. They cannot then be distinguished from genuine components.

cards.f: A 7 kHz tone is sampled at 10 kHz. At what frequency does it appear?
Why must an anti-aliasing filter be analogue and placed before the ADC?
cards.b: Once the signal is sampled, aliased components overlap genuine ones and cannot be removed digitally. They must be attenuated before sampling.

cards.f: Give the Fourier series of a ±A square wave (odd symmetry).
cards.b: x(t) = (4A/π)Σ (1/n)sin(nω0t) over odd n only.

cards.f: State Parseval's theorem for a periodic signal.
cards.b: The average power equals the sum of the squared magnitudes of the exponential Fourier coefficients: P = Σ|cn|².

cards.f: What is the Gibbs phenomenon?
cards.b: Near a jump discontinuity, Fourier partial sums overshoot by about 9% of the jump. The overshoot narrows as more terms are added but does not shrink in height.

cards.f: What is the frequency resolution of an N-point DFT at sampling rate fs?
cards.b: Δf = fs/N. For example, 8 kHz and N = 256 give 31.25 Hz per bin.

cards.f: Which harmonics are present in a signal with half-wave symmetry x(t + T0/2) = −x(t)?
cards.b: Only odd harmonics. There is no DC term and no even harmonics.

cards.f: Why is a window such as Hann applied before an FFT?
cards.b: It tapers the record ends, which reduces spectral leakage when a tone does not complete a whole number of cycles in the record. The cost is a wider main lobe.

questions.q: What is the average power (normalised to 1 Ω) of x(t) = 4 cos(200πt + π/3)?
questions.why: A sinusoid of amplitude A has average power A²/2 = 16/2 = 8 W. The phase and frequency do not affect it.

questions.q: Evaluate ∫ cos(t)·δ(t − π) dt over all t.
questions.why: By the sifting property, the integral equals cos(π) = −1.

questions.q: A 5-sample sequence is convolved with a 3-sample sequence. How many samples does the result have?
questions.why: Linear convolution of lengths N and M gives N + M − 1 = 5 + 3 − 1 = 7 samples.

questions.q: What is the Laplace transform of e^(−3t)u(t)?
questions.why: e^(−at)u(t) transforms to 1/(s + a), so with a = 3 the result is 1/(s + 3).

questions.q: The output of a stable system has Y(s) = 5/(s(s + 2)(s + 5)). What is the final value of y(t)?
questions.why: sY(s) has poles only at −2 and −5, so the final value theorem applies: lim as s → 0 of 5/((s + 2)(s + 5)) = 5/10 = 0.5.

questions.q: Above its natural frequency, what is the asymptotic magnitude slope of an underdamped second-order low-pass system?
questions.why: Two poles each contribute −20 dB/decade, giving −40 dB/decade (about −12 dB/octave) whatever the damping.

questions.q: A standard second-order closed loop has damping ratio ζ = 0.7. What is the approximate percentage overshoot of its step response?
An open-loop frequency response has |L(jω)| = 1 at a frequency where ∠L(jω) = −135°. What is the phase margin?
Which term of a PID controller removes steady-state error to a step input for a type-0 plant?
questions.why: Integral action adds a pole at the origin, making the loop type 1, so step error goes to zero.

questions.q: A telephone speech signal is band-limited to 3.4 kHz. What sampling rate does the sampling theorem require?
questions.why: The sampling rate must exceed twice the highest frequency, 2 × 3.4 = 6.8 kHz. Telephony uses 8 kHz to leave room for the anti-aliasing filter.

questions.q: Classify x1(t) = 3e^(−2|t|) and x2(t) = 2 cos(100πt) + cos(300πt) as energy or power signals, and find the energy or power of each.
markScheme: x1: E = 9∫e^(−4|t|) dt = 9 × 2/4 = 4.5, so it is an energy signal.
x2: periodic sum of sinusoids at distinct frequencies, so it is a power signal.
questions.modelAnswer: For x1, |x1|² = 9e^(−4|t|), which is even. So E = 2 × 9∫ from 0 to ∞ of e^(−4t) dt = 18/4 = 4.5 (normalised). The energy is finite, so x1 is an energy signal with zero average power. x2 is a sum of sinusoids at 50 Hz and 150 Hz, which persist forever, so it is a power signal. The frequencies differ, so the powers add: 4/2 + 1/2 = 2.5 W. The signal is periodic with T0 = 20 ms.

questions.q: An LTI system has impulse response h(t) = 2e^(−3t)u(t). Find its unit step response and its final value.
markScheme: Step response s(t) = ∫ from 0 to t of h(τ) dτ.
Final value = 2/3, which equals the DC gain ∫h dt.
questions.modelAnswer: The step response is the running integral of the impulse response. For t > 0, s(t) = ∫ from 0 to t of 2e^(−3τ) dτ = (2/3)(1 − e^(−3t)), and s(t) = 0 for t < 0. It rises with a time constant of 1/3 s towards a final value of 2/3. This equals the DC gain ∫h dt = 2/3, or H(0) where H(s) = 2/(s + 3). The system is causal and BIBO stable because ∫|h| dt is finite.

questions.q: The amplitude modulator y(t) = x(t)cos(ω0 t) is used in a radio transmitter. State, with brief reasons, whether it is linear, time-invariant, causal, memoryless and BIBO stable.
markScheme: Linear: a sum of inputs gives the sum of outputs, so superposition holds.
Time-varying: a delayed input gives x(t − T)cos(ω0 t), not x(t − T)cos(ω0(t − T)).
Causal: depends only on the present input.
Memoryless: output at t depends only on x(t).
BIBO stable: |y| ≤ |x|, so a bounded input gives a bounded output.
questions.modelAnswer: The system is linear, because (ax1 + bx2)cos ω0t = ay1 + by2. It is time-varying: delaying the input gives x(t − T)cos ω0t, while the delayed output is x(t − T)cos ω0(t − T), and these differ. It is causal and memoryless, since y(t) depends only on x at the same instant. It is BIBO stable because |cos| ≤ 1, so |y(t)| ≤ |x(t)|. Being time-varying is exactly what lets it shift spectra to new frequencies, which no LTI system can do.

questions.q: Find the inverse Laplace transform of F(s) = (s + 3)/((s + 1)(s + 2)).
questions.modelAnswer: Use partial fractions with the cover-up rule. For the pole at s = −1, cover (s + 1) and substitute: A = (−1 + 3)/(−1 + 2) = 2. For s = −2: B = (−2 + 3)/(−2 + 1) = −1. So F(s) = 2/(s + 1) − 1/(s + 2), and f(t) = (2e^(−t) − e^(−2t))u(t). Check: f(0⁺) = 1, which matches the initial value theorem since sF(s) → 1 as s → ∞.

questions.q: A position servo has G(s) = 10/(s² + 2s + 10). Find its poles, ωn, ζ, DC gain and the percentage overshoot of its step response.
questions.modelAnswer: Completing the square gives (s + 1)² + 9, so the poles are at −1 ± j3. Comparing with s² + 2ζωn s + ωn² gives ωn = √10 = 3.16 rad/s and ζ = 1/√10 = 0.316. The DC gain is G(0) = 1. The overshoot exponent is ζπ/√(1 − ζ²) = σπ/ωd = π/3, so %OS = 100e^(−1.047) = 35.1%. The peak occurs at π/ωd = π/3 = 1.05 s.

questions.q: An RC low-pass filter uses R = 1.6 kΩ and C = 100 nF. Find its cutoff frequency in Hz and its gain in dB at 10 kHz.
questions.modelAnswer: RC = 1.6 × 10³ × 100 × 10⁻⁹ = 1.6 × 10⁻⁴ s, so fc = 1/(2π × 1.6 × 10⁻⁴) = 995 Hz. At 10 kHz, f/fc = 10.05, so |H| = 1/√(1 + 101) = 0.099, which is about −20.1 dB. This matches the −20 dB/decade asymptote one decade above the corner. The phase there is about −84°.

questions.q: A plant G(s) = 20/(s + 4) is under unity-feedback proportional control with gain 1. Find the steady-state error to a unit step and the closed-loop time constant, and compare with the open-loop time constant.
markScheme: Closed loop: T = 20/(s + 24), so the pole is at −24 and τ = 1/24 s ≈ 41.7 ms.
Open loop τ = 0.25 s, so feedback speeds the response by a factor of 6.
questions.modelAnswer: The loop is type 0 with Kp = L(0) = 20/4 = 5, so the unit-step error is 1/(1 + Kp) = 1/6 = 0.167. The closed loop is T = G/(1 + G) = 20/(s + 24). Its single pole is at −24, so τ = 41.7 ms, compared with 1/4 = 0.25 s open loop. Feedback has made the response six times faster, at the cost of an offset that only integral action or higher gain can reduce.

questions.q: Use the Routh–Hurwitz criterion to determine how many roots of s³ + s² + s + 2 = 0 lie in the right half-plane.
markScheme: First column 1, 1, −1, 2 has two sign changes, so there are two RHP roots.
questions.modelAnswer: The s³ row is 1, 1 and the s² row is 1, 2. The s¹ entry is (1 × 1 − 1 × 2)/1 = −1 and the s⁰ entry is 2. The first column reads 1, 1, −1, 2, with two sign changes, so two roots lie in the right half-plane. (They are a complex pair at about 0.18 ± j1.20; the third root is near −1.35.) All the coefficients are positive, yet the polynomial is unstable: the sign test alone is not enough beyond second order.

questions.q: A loop under proportional control oscillates steadily at Ku = 8 with period Pu = 2 s. Give Ziegler–Nichols PI settings in both standard and parallel form.
questions.modelAnswer: The Ziegler–Nichols ultimate-gain rules for PI are Kp = 0.45Ku and Ti = Pu/1.2. With Ku = 8 and Pu = 2 s, Kp = 3.6 and Ti = 1.67 s. In parallel form, Ki = Kp/Ti = 3.6/1.667 = 2.16 s⁻¹, so C(s) = 3.6 + 2.16/s. These settings are fairly aggressive, so they should be checked by simulation or a small step test before use.

questions.q: An audio system samples at 44.1 kHz. (a) What is the Nyquist frequency? (b) Where would an unfiltered 25 kHz ultrasonic tone appear? (c) What is the bin spacing of a 4096-point FFT?
markScheme: 25 kHz exceeds 22.05 kHz, so it aliases.
Alias at |25 − 44.1| = 19.1 kHz, within the audible band.
questions.modelAnswer: The Nyquist frequency is fs/2 = 22.05 kHz. A 25 kHz tone lies above it, so after sampling it folds to |25 − 44.1| = 19.1 kHz. That is an audible artefact which cannot be removed afterwards, so the analogue anti-aliasing filter must pass the audio band up to 20 kHz yet attenuate strongly above 22.05 kHz (anything above 24.1 kHz folds back below 20 kHz), a very narrow transition band. A 4096-point FFT gives a bin spacing of 44 100/4096 = 10.8 Hz and covers a record of about 93 ms.

questions.q: Maya is characterising signals for a data-acquisition course. (a) Find the energy of x1(t) = 3e^(−2|t|). (b) For x2(t) = 2 cos(100πt) + cos(300πt), find the fundamental period and the average power. (c) Find the average power of the unit step u(t) and say whether it is an energy or power signal. (d) Find the even and odd parts of x3(t) = e^(−t)u(t). (e) Determine whether x4[n] = cos(3πn/8) is periodic and, if so, its fundamental period.
markScheme: (b) Frequencies 50 Hz and 150 Hz; ratio 3, which is rational.
(c) P = lim (1/2T)∫ from 0 to T of 1 dt = 1/2.
(c) Infinite energy but finite power, so it is a power signal.
(e) Ω0/(2π) = 3/16, which is rational, so the signal is periodic.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) |x1|² = 9e^(−4|t|) is even, so E = 2 × 9∫ from 0 to ∞ of e^(−4t) dt = 18 × ¼ = 4.5. The energy is finite, so x1 is an energy signal and its average power is zero.

(b) The two components are at 50 Hz (period 20 ms) and 150 Hz (period 6.67 ms). Their frequency ratio is 3, which is rational, so the sum is periodic. The fundamental frequency is the highest common factor, 50 Hz, so T0 = 20 ms. The frequencies are distinct, so the cross terms average to zero and the powers add: P = 4/2 + 1/2 = 2.5 W (normalised to 1 Ω).

(c) For u(t), P = lim as T → ∞ of (1/2T)∫ from −T to T of u² dt = lim T/(2T) = 1/2. The energy ∫ from 0 to ∞ of 1 dt is infinite, so u(t) is a power signal, even though it is not periodic.

(d) x3(−t) = e^(t)u(−t). So xe(t) = ½[e^(−t)u(t) + e^(t)u(−t)] = ½e^(−|t|), and xo(t) = ½[e^(−t)u(t) − e^(t)u(−t)] = ½sgn(t)e^(−|t|). Check: xe + xo is e^(−t) for t > 0 and 0 for t < 0, which is x3. At t = 0 both parts take the value ½ by convention, so the sum is the midpoint value of the step.

(e) cos(Ω0 n) is periodic only if Ω0/(2π) is rational. Here Ω0/(2π) = (3π/8)/(2π) = 3/16, which is rational in lowest terms, so N = 16 samples (covering exactly 3 cycles of the underlying cosine). By contrast, the continuous signal cos(3πt/8) has period 16/3 s, which is not an integer. This shows that discrete-time periodicity has to be checked separately.

questions.q: Oliver is studying a digital smoothing filter described by y[n] = 0.5y[n − 1] + x[n], initially at rest. (a) Find its impulse response h[n] and state whether it is causal and BIBO stable. (b) Find the step response in closed form and evaluate it for n = 0 to 3. (c) Find the output for the input x[n] = δ[n] + δ[n − 1]. (d) Oliver also considers three continuous-time systems: S1: y(t) = t·x(t); S2: y(t) = x²(t); S3: y(t) = x(t + 1). Classify each as linear or not, time-invariant or not, and causal or not, with justification.
markScheme: Iterating with x = δ: h[0] = 1, h[1] = 0.5, ..., so h[n] = 0.5ⁿu[n].
Causal since h[n] = 0 for n < 0; stable since Σ|h| = 1/(1 − 0.5) = 2 is finite.
Step response s[n] = Σ from k = 0 to n of 0.5ᵏ = 2(1 − 0.5ⁿ⁺¹) = 2 − 0.5ⁿ.
Input δ[n] + δ[n − 1] gives h[n] + h[n − 1] by linearity and time invariance.
S3: linear, time-invariant, non-causal (predicts the future).
Justifications use the formal tests, such as delaying the input against delaying the output.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Set x[n] = δ[n] with y[−1] = 0. Then h[0] = 1, h[1] = 0.5, h[2] = 0.25, and in general h[n] = 0.5ⁿu[n]. It is causal, since h[n] = 0 for n < 0. It is BIBO stable, since Σ|h[n]| = 1/(1 − 0.5) = 2 is finite. Equivalently, its only pole, at z = 0.5, lies inside the unit circle.

(b) The step response is the running sum of h: s[n] = Σ from k = 0 to n of 0.5ᵏ = (1 − 0.5ⁿ⁺¹)/(1 − 0.5) = 2 − 0.5ⁿ for n ≥ 0. So s[0] = 1, s[1] = 1.5, s[2] = 1.75 and s[3] = 1.875, approaching the DC gain of 2. A direct check from the recursion: y[1] = 0.5 × 1 + 1 = 1.5.

(c) By linearity and time invariance, y[n] = h[n] + h[n − 1]. This gives y[0] = 1, y[1] = 0.5 + 1 = 1.5, y[2] = 0.25 + 0.5 = 0.75 and y[3] = 0.375. For n ≥ 1, y[n] = 0.5ⁿ + 0.5ⁿ⁻¹ = 3(0.5ⁿ).

(d) S1, y = t·x(t): scaling and adding inputs scales and adds outputs, so it is linear. A delayed input gives t·x(t − T), but the delayed output is (t − T)x(t − T), so it is time-varying. It uses only the present input, so it is causal.

S2, y = x²: doubling the input quadruples the output, so it is non-linear. A delayed input gives x²(t − T), which equals the delayed output, so it is time-invariant. It is causal and memoryless.

S3, y = x(t + 1): this is linear and time-invariant (a pure time advance). It is not causal, because the output at t needs the input at t + 1. It is realisable offline on recorded data but not in real time. Its impulse response δ(t + 1) is non-zero at t = −1, which confirms non-causality.

questions.q: A sensor's dynamics obey y″ + 3y′ + 2y = 3u(t), where u(t) is the unit step. At t = 0 the output is y(0) = 1 and y′(0) = 0. (a) Take Laplace transforms, including the initial conditions, and find Y(s). (b) Use partial fractions to find y(t). (c) Verify both initial conditions. (d) Use the final value theorem to find y(∞), justifying its use. (e) Identify the natural (transient) and forced parts of the response, and evaluate y(1).
markScheme: FVT valid because the poles of sY are at −1 and −2 (LHP); y(∞) = 3/2.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Using L{y′} = sY − y(0) and L{y″} = s²Y − s·y(0) − y′(0) with y(0) = 1 and y′(0) = 0:
(s²Y − s) + 3(sY − 1) + 2Y = 3/s
So (s² + 3s + 2)Y = s + 3 + 3/s, and Y(s) = (s² + 3s + 3)/(s(s + 1)(s + 2)).

(b) Write Y = A/s + B/(s + 1) + C/(s + 2). The cover-up rule gives:
- A = 3/((1)(2)) = 1.5
- B = (1 − 3 + 3)/((−1)(1)) = −1
- C = (4 − 6 + 3)/((−2)(−1)) = 0.5
So y(t) = 1.5 − e^(−t) + 0.5e^(−2t) for t ≥ 0.

(c) y(0) = 1.5 − 1 + 0.5 = 1, as required. y′(t) = e^(−t) − e^(−2t), so y′(0) = 0, as required. Substituting into the ODE as a further check: y″ = −e^(−t) + 2e^(−2t), so y″ + 3y′ + 2y = (−1 + 3 − 2)e^(−t) + (2 − 3 + 1)e^(−2t) + 3 = 3. Correct.

(d) sY(s) = (s² + 3s + 3)/((s + 1)(s + 2)) has poles only at −1 and −2, both in the left half-plane, so the final value theorem applies: y(∞) = 3/2 = 1.5. This agrees with setting the derivatives to zero in the ODE: 2y = 3.

(e) The forced (steady-state) response is the constant 1.5, set by the step input and the DC gain 3/2. The natural response −e^(−t) + 0.5e^(−2t) consists of the system's modes, at the poles −1 and −2, and decays to zero. The slow mode e^(−t) dominates after about a second. At t = 1, y = 1.5 − 0.368 + 0.068 = 1.20.

The initial conditions change only the weights of the natural modes, not the modes themselves or the forced value. That is why the poles alone decide stability.

questions.q: A vibration-isolation mount is modelled as a mass m = 2 kg on a spring k = 50 N/m with a damper b = 8 N s/m. A force F(t) acts on the mass and x(t) is its displacement, starting from rest. (a) Derive the transfer function X(s)/F(s). (b) Find the poles, ωn and ζ. (c) For a 10 N step force, find the final displacement, the percentage overshoot, the peak displacement and its time, and the 2% settling time. (d) Engineer Daniel wants the fastest response with no overshoot. What damping coefficient is needed, and what happens to the final displacement?
markScheme: Newton's second law: m x″ + b x′ + k x = F, giving X/F = 1/(2s² + 8s + 50).
DC gain 1/k = 0.02 m/N; final x = 0.2 m.
Final displacement unchanged at 0.2 m because it depends only on k.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Newton's second law gives m x″ = F − b x′ − k x, so 2x″ + 8x′ + 50x = F. With zero initial conditions, X(s)/F(s) = 1/(2s² + 8s + 50) = 0.5/(s² + 4s + 25).

(b) The poles are the roots of s² + 4s + 25 = 0: s = −2 ± j√21 = −2 ± j4.58. Comparing with s² + 2ζωn s + ωn² gives ωn = 5 rad/s and 2ζωn = 4, so ζ = 0.4 (underdamped). The damped frequency is ωd = 4.58 rad/s.

(c) The DC gain is 1/k = 0.02 m/N, so a 10 N step gives a final displacement of 0.2 m (the static spring deflection F/k). The overshoot is %OS = 100e^(−ζπ/√(1 − ζ²)) = 100e^(−0.4π/0.917) = 25.4%. The peak displacement is 0.2 × 1.254 = 0.251 m, at tp = π/ωd = π/4.583 = 0.686 s. The 2% settling time is about 4/(ζωn) = 4/2 = 2 s, since the envelope is e^(−2t).

(d) Critical damping requires ζ = 1, so b = 2√(km) = 2√(50 × 2) = 20 N s/m. The poles then coincide at s = −5, and the step response 0.2[1 − (1 + 5t)e^(−5t)] rises without overshoot. It takes about 5.8/ωn ≈ 1.2 s to come within 2%, faster than the underdamped case's 2 s settling. The final displacement stays at 0.2 m, because at steady state the velocity is zero and the damper carries no force, so only k matters.

In isolation applications there is a trade-off. Heavier damping suppresses resonance near ωn, but it transmits more force at high frequencies. Daniel should check the frequency response as well as the step response.

questions.q: Aisha must sketch the Bode plot of G(s) = 10(s + 10)/((s + 1)(s + 100)). (a) Rewrite G in time-constant (Bode) form and find the DC gain in dB. (b) List the corner frequencies and describe the straight-line magnitude asymptotes, giving their levels at ω = 1, 10, 100 and 1000 rad/s. (c) Calculate the exact magnitude (dB) and phase at ω = 10 rad/s and compare with the asymptote. (d) Describe the overall phase trend and the filter type this represents.
markScheme: Corners: pole at 1, zero at 10, pole at 100 rad/s.
Asymptote: 0 dB up to 1; −20 dB/decade to −20 dB at 10.
Flat at −20 dB from 10 to 100; then −20 dB/decade, reaching −40 dB at 1000.
Difference of about +3 dB from the zero at its own corner (the other corners contribute little).
Phase trend: 0° at DC, dipping (about −40° at 1, −45° at 10, −50° at 100), towards −90° at high frequency.
Identifies a low-pass response with a shelf (lag-type network).
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Normalise each factor: s + 10 = 10(1 + s/10), s + 1 = (1 + s) and s + 100 = 100(1 + s/100). Then G = 10 × 10(1 + s/10)/(100(1 + s)(1 + s/100)) = (1 + s/10)/((1 + s)(1 + s/100)). The DC gain is 1, which is 0 dB.

(b) The corner frequencies are a pole at 1 rad/s, a zero at 10 rad/s and a pole at 100 rad/s. The straight-line asymptote is:
- 0 dB up to ω = 1;
- −20 dB/decade from 1 to 10, reaching −20 dB at ω = 10;
- flat at −20 dB from 10 to 100, as the zero cancels the slope;
- −20 dB/decade above 100, reaching −40 dB at 1000.
So the levels are 0, −20, −20 and −40 dB at ω = 1, 10, 100 and 1000.

(c) At ω = 10:
|G| = |1 + j|/(|1 + j10| × |1 + j0.1|) = 1.414/(10.05 × 1.005) = 0.140, which is −17.1 dB.
This is about 3 dB above the −20 dB asymptote, because the zero contributes its +3 dB correction at its own corner, while the poles at 1 and 100 are a decade away and contribute only about −0.04 dB each.
Phase = arctan(1) − arctan(10) − arctan(0.1) = 45° − 84.3° − 5.7° = −45°.

(d) The phase starts at 0°. The pole at 1 pulls it to about −40° by ω = 1. The zero at 10 holds it near −45° to −50° through the shelf region (exact values: −45° at 10 and −50.1° at 100). Above 100 the second pole takes it towards −90° (−84.8° at 1000). The overall response is low-pass with an intermediate shelf of −20 dB, the shape of a lag network. Exact magnitudes are −3.0 dB at ω = 1, −23.0 dB at ω = 100 and −40.0 dB at ω = 1000, all within about 3 dB of the asymptotes.

questions.q: A resonant actuator has G(s) = ωn²/(s² + 2ζωn s + ωn²) with ωn = 100 rad/s and ζ = 0.2. (a) Find the resonant peak magnitude (linear and dB) and the frequency at which it occurs; confirm by evaluating |G| at ωn. (b) Find the −3 dB bandwidth. (c) Find the magnitude (dB) and phase at 1000 rad/s, and compare with the asymptote. (d) Relate the peak to the step-response overshoot. (e) Sam proposes raising ζ to 0.7. Discuss what changes in the frequency and time domains and the physical trade-offs.
markScheme: At 1000 rad/s: |G| ≈ 0.0101, which is −39.9 dB, close to the −40 dB asymptote (−40 dB/decade above ωn).
Step overshoot = e^(−ζπ/√(1 − ζ²)) = 52.7%; a large Mr goes with a large overshoot.
ζ = 0.7: Mr ≈ 1.0002 (essentially none, since 0.7 is just below 1/√2), bandwidth ≈ ωn, overshoot 4.6%.
Trade-offs: more damping means more energy dissipated, possible extra actuator effort or sensor noise, and a slower initial rise.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) ζ = 0.2 is below 1/√2, so a resonant peak exists:
Mr = 1/(2ζ√(1 − ζ²)) = 1/(0.4 × 0.9798) = 2.55, which is 20 log₁₀ 2.55 = 8.14 dB.
It occurs at ωr = ωn√(1 − 2ζ²) = 100√0.92 = 95.9 rad/s. At ωn itself the denominator is j2ζωn², so |G| = 1/(2ζ) = 2.5 (7.96 dB) with phase exactly −90°, slightly below the peak, as expected.

(b) Setting |G| = 1/√2 gives ωb = ωn√(1 − 2ζ² + √(4ζ⁴ − 4ζ² + 2)) = 100√(0.92 + √1.8464) = 100√2.279 = 151 rad/s.

(c) At ω = 1000 = 10ωn, the denominator is (ωn² − ω²) + j2ζωnω = −990 000 + j40 000. Then |G| = 10 000/990 808 = 0.0101, which is −39.9 dB. The phase is −180° + arctan(40 000/990 000) = −177.7°. The asymptote falls at −40 dB/decade from 0 dB at ωn, giving −40 dB at 1000 rad/s, so the agreement is close.

(d) Low damping shows up in both domains. The step overshoot is e^(−ζπ/√(1 − ζ²)) = e^(−0.641) = 52.7%, with ringing at ωd = 98 rad/s. A large Mr in the frequency domain corresponds to a large overshoot in the step response. Disturbances near 96 rad/s are amplified 2.55 times.

(e) With ζ = 0.7, Mr = 1/(1.4 × 0.714) ≈ 1.0002, essentially flat, because 0.7 is just below 0.707. The bandwidth becomes ωn√(0.02 + √2.0004) ≈ 1.0 × ωn = 100 rad/s, and the overshoot falls to 4.6%, with settling time about 4/(ζωn) = 57 ms instead of 200 ms.

The costs: added damping must come from somewhere. A passive damper dissipates energy and heat, and active damping through velocity feedback needs a velocity sensor and extra actuator effort, and it injects sensor noise. The lower bandwidth also slows the response to fast commands. A ζ of about 0.7 is a common compromise, giving a maximally flat response with small overshoot.

questions.q: A camera gimbal axis has open-loop transfer function L(s) = K/(s(s + 4)) under unity feedback. (a) Find the closed-loop transfer function and the value of K that gives ζ = 0.5. (b) For this K, find ωn, the percentage overshoot, the peak time and the 2% settling time. (c) Find the steady-state errors to a unit step and a unit ramp. (d) The operator, Jess, wants the ramp-tracking error reduced fourfold by raising K. Find the new K and recompute ζ, overshoot and settling time. Comment on the result and suggest a better approach.
markScheme: 2ζωn = 4 and ωn² = K; ζ = 0.5 gives ωn = 4, so K = 16.
Fourfold reduction needs Kv = 16, so K = 64: ωn = 8, ζ = 0.25.
Overshoot rises to 44.4%; ts stays ≈ 2 s because ζωn = 2 is unchanged.
Suggests lag compensation (or PI) to raise low-frequency gain without moving the dominant poles; or lead compensation.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) T(s) = L/(1 + L) = K/(s² + 4s + K). Matching the standard form gives ωn² = K and 2ζωn = 4. For ζ = 0.5, ωn = 4 rad/s, so K = 16.

(b) With ωn = 4 rad/s and ζ = 0.5:
- %OS = 100e^(−0.5π/0.866) = 16.3%
- tp = π/(ωn√(1 − ζ²)) = π/3.464 = 0.907 s
- ts ≈ 4/(ζωn) = 4/2 = 2 s

(c) L has one integrator, so the loop is type 1 and the unit-step error is zero. The velocity constant is Kv = lim sL(s) = K/4 = 4 s⁻¹, so a unit ramp (1 rad/s) leaves a lag of 1/Kv = 0.25 rad.

(d) A fourfold reduction needs Kv = 16, so K = 64. Then ωn = 8 rad/s and ζ = 4/16 = 0.25. The overshoot becomes 100e^(−0.25π/0.968) = 44.4%, and the peak time falls to π/(8 × 0.968) = 0.41 s. The settling time stays at about 4/(ζωn) = 2 s, because the real part of the poles is fixed at −2 by the plant's damping term: only the imaginary part grows.

The tracking improves, but the gimbal would overshoot by 44% and ring visibly, which is unacceptable for camera stabilisation. Gain alone cannot set ζ and Kv independently in this loop.

A better approach is a lag compensator, C(s) = (s + z)/(s + p) with z/p = 4 and both placed well below the crossover frequency (for example z = 0.2, p = 0.05). It raises the low-frequency gain, and hence Kv, by four while leaving the dominant poles near ζ = 0.5. PI control would go further and remove the ramp error altogether, since it makes the loop type 2, but it needs care with stability. Alternatively, a lead compensator could add phase margin so that a higher K remains well damped.

questions.q: A heater process has transfer function G(s) = 10/(s + 2) from drive signal to temperature rise (normalised units), controlled by a proportional gain K with unity feedback. (a) Find the step steady-state error as a function of K and choose K for a 2% error. (b) Find the closed-loop pole and time constant for this K and compare with the open loop. (c) Evaluate the sensitivity at DC and estimate the effect on the closed-loop DC gain of a 10% rise in plant gain; verify exactly. (d) For a unit step setpoint, find the initial and final controller outputs and discuss the practical implication. (e) Explain how adding integral action would change parts (a) and (c).
markScheme: Closed loop: T = 10K/(s + 2 + 10K) = 98/(s + 100); pole −100, τ = 10 ms.
Open-loop τ = 0.5 s, so 50 times faster.
10% plant change gives ≈ 0.02 × 10% = 0.2% change in T(0).
50:1 peak-to-steady drive ratio implies actuator saturation and a slower real response; noise amplification.
Integral action: zero steady-state error and S(0) = 0, so the DC gain is insensitive to plant gain; note windup.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The DC plant gain is G(0) = 5, so Kp = 5K and the unit-step error is 1/(1 + 5K). For 2%, 1 + 5K = 50, so K = 9.8.

(b) T(s) = KG/(1 + KG) = 98/(s + 2 + 98) = 98/(s + 100). The closed-loop pole is at −100, so τ = 10 ms, compared with 0.5 s open loop: fifty times faster. The DC gain is 0.98, consistent with the 2% error.

(c) S(0) = 1/(1 + L(0)) = 1/50 = 0.02. Since dT/T ≈ S·dG/G, a 10% rise in plant gain should change T(0) by about 0.2%. Exactly: L(0) becomes 9.8 × 5.5 = 53.9, so T(0) = 53.9/54.9 = 0.9818 against 0.9800, a 0.18% change. Feedback has reduced the effect of plant uncertainty about fiftyfold.

(d) At t = 0⁺ the output is still zero, so e = 1 and u = 9.8. In steady state e = 0.02, so u = 0.196, which is just what the plant needs to hold 0.98 (0.98/5 = 0.196). The controller briefly demands 50 times its steady drive. A real heater driver would saturate, so the true response would be limited by actuator power, not by the 10 ms time constant. The high gain also amplifies sensor noise by about K. In practice K would be reduced, or the setpoint ramped or pre-filtered.

(e) With PI control, C = K(1 + 1/(Ti s)), the loop becomes type 1. The step error then goes to zero for any stabilising gain, so the large K is no longer needed for accuracy. S(0) becomes 0, so the closed-loop DC gain is exactly 1 whatever the plant gain. Choosing Ti = 0.5 s to cancel the plant pole gives a first-order closed loop with a time constant set by the designer. The penalties are possible integrator windup during saturation, which needs anti-windup, and some loss of phase margin if Ti is made too small.

questions.q: A robot joint has open-loop transfer function L(s) = K/(s(s + 1)(s + 5)) with unity feedback. (a) Use the Routh–Hurwitz criterion to find the range of K for closed-loop stability. (b) Find the frequency of sustained oscillation at the stability limit and the closed-loop poles there. (c) For K = 10, find the gain margin (linear and dB) and the phase margin, showing how each is obtained. (d) Estimate the closed-loop damping ratio from the phase margin and comment on suitability. (e) Explain what an additional pure time delay of 0.2 s would do to the margins.
markScheme: Routh: s³: 1, 5; s²: 6, K; s¹: (30 − K)/6; s⁰: K.
At K = 30: auxiliary 6s² + 30 = 0, so ω = √5 = 2.24 rad/s; third pole at −6.
Phase crossover where ∠L = −180°: arctan ω + arctan(ω/5) = 90°, so ω² = 5, ω = 2.24 rad/s.
|L| there = K/30, so GM = 3, which is 9.54 dB, for K = 10.
Gain crossover: 10 = ω√(ω² + 1)√(ω² + 25), so ω ≈ 1.23 rad/s.
ζ ≈ PM/100 ≈ 0.25: lightly damped with large overshoot (about 49% simulated); target PM of 45–60°.
Delay adds −ωT phase: about −14° at 1.23 rad/s, so PM falls to about 11°; the phase crossover moves lower, reducing GM.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) 1 + L = 0 gives s³ + 6s² + 5s + K = 0. The Routh array is:
- s³: 1, 5
- s²: 6, K
- s¹: (30 − K)/6
- s⁰: K
No sign changes requires K > 0 and 30 − K > 0, so 0 < K < 30.

(b) At K = 30 the s¹ row vanishes. The auxiliary polynomial from the s² row is 6s² + 30 = 0, giving s = ±j√5. The loop oscillates at 2.24 rad/s (period 2.81 s). Dividing the cubic by s² + 5 leaves (s + 6), so the closed-loop poles are −6 and ±j2.24.

(c) The phase is ∠L = −90° − arctan ω − arctan(ω/5). It reaches −180° when arctan ω + arctan(ω/5) = 90°, which means ω × ω/5 = 1, so ω = √5. There |L| = K/(√5 × √6 × √30) = K/30. For K = 10, GM = 30/10 = 3, which is 9.54 dB, consistent with part (a).

The gain crossover requires 10 = ω√(ω² + 1)√(ω² + 25). Solving numerically gives ω ≈ 1.23 rad/s. The phase there is −90° − 50.8° − 13.8° = −154.6°, so PM ≈ 25.4°.

(d) Using ζ ≈ PM/100 gives ζ ≈ 0.25, which suggests overshoot approaching 50% (a step simulation of this loop gives about 49%) and pronounced ringing. Most servo specifications ask for a PM of 45–60°. K should therefore be reduced, or a lead compensator added, which brings phase lead at about 1–2 rad/s.

(e) A delay e^(−0.2s) has unit magnitude but adds a lag of 0.2ω rad. At the 1.23 rad/s crossover that is 0.246 rad = 14.1°, so the PM drops to about 11°, close to instability. The −180° crossing also moves down from 2.24 rad/s, to where |L| is larger, so the gain margin shrinks too. The delay erodes both margins without changing the magnitude plot, which is why delays (from communication, computation or sensors) are dangerous in high-bandwidth loops.

questions.q: Nadia is stabilising an inverted-pendulum-like system whose loop transfer function is L(s) = K(s + 1)/(s(s − 1)(s + 6)), with one open-loop pole in the right half-plane. (a) Form the characteristic polynomial and use Routh–Hurwitz to find all K for which the closed loop is stable. (b) Find the frequency of oscillation at the stability boundary. (c) For K = 15, find the closed-loop poles and comment on the damping. (d) Show that at K = 15 the phase-crossover magnitude is |L| = 2, and interpret this as a gain margin. Explain why a conventional 'gain margin' reading would mislead here. (e) Use the Nyquist criterion to explain what the Nyquist plot must do for stability, and why the zero at −1 is essential.
markScheme: Characteristic polynomial: s(s − 1)(s + 6) + K(s + 1) = s³ + 5s² + (K − 6)s + K.
At K = 7.5: auxiliary 5s² + 7.5 = 0, so ω = √1.5 = 1.22 rad/s.
Dominant pair ζ ≈ 0.67/2.02 ≈ 0.33; the zero at −1 makes the overshoot much larger (about 90%), so the design needs refining.
Interpretation: gain can be reduced by a factor of 2 (6.0 dB) before instability; a lower gain margin, so the system is conditionally stable.
Reading |L| > 1 at −180° as 'unstable' would be wrong because P = 1.
Nyquist: Z = N + P with P = 1, so stability needs N = −1, one anticlockwise encirclement of −1.
Without the zero, the polynomial s³ + 5s² − 6s + K has a negative coefficient and is unstable for all K; the zero supplies phase lead.
Links the minimum gain to the need for enough loop gain to pull the RHP pole across.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) 1 + L = 0 gives s(s − 1)(s + 6) + K(s + 1) = s³ + 5s² + (K − 6)s + K = 0. The Routh array is:
- s³: 1, K − 6
- s²: 5, K
- s¹: [5(K − 6) − K]/5 = (4K − 30)/5
- s⁰: K
All first-column entries are positive when K > 7.5, with no upper limit.

(b) At K = 7.5 the auxiliary polynomial 5s² + 7.5 = 0 gives s = ±j1.22 rad/s (third pole at −5).

(c) For K = 15, s³ + 5s² + 9s + 15 has roots −3.66 and −0.67 ± j1.91. The dominant pair has ζ = 0.67/2.02 = 0.33. The closed-loop zero at −1 lies near these poles and greatly raises the peak: a step simulation gives about 90% overshoot, so further compensation is needed.

(d) At ω = 1.22 rad/s the phase of L is −180° (the boundary frequency), and:
|L| = 15 × |1 + j1.22|/(1.22 × |j1.22 − 1| × |6 + j1.22|) = 15 × 1.58/(1.22 × 1.58 × 6.12) = 2.0.
Instability occurs if K falls to 7.5, half of 15, so the margin is a gain reduction of 2 (6.0 dB). The usual rule that |L| < 1 at −180° means stability does not apply to an open-loop unstable plant, so reading |L| = 2 as 'unstable' would be wrong. Actuator saturation, which effectively lowers the gain, could destabilise the loop.

(e) Nyquist: Z = N + P with P = 1, so stability needs N = −1: the plot (indented round the origin pole) must encircle −1 once anticlockwise, which requires it to cross the negative real axis left of −1, i.e. K > 7.5.

Without the zero, s³ + 5s² − 6s + K has a negative coefficient and is unstable for all K. The zero at −1 supplies the phase lead that makes the encirclement possible, which is why unstable plants need lead action as well as enough gain.

questions.q: Ben is tuning a PID controller for a motor-driven conveyor with plant P(s) = 1/(s(s + 1)(s + 5)). Under proportional-only control the loop oscillates steadily at Ku = 30. (a) Find the ultimate period Pu. (b) Give the Ziegler–Nichols PID settings in standard (Kp, Ti, Td) and parallel (Kp, Ki, Kd) form. (c) Form the closed-loop characteristic polynomial and, given that its roots are approximately −4.13, −1.12 and −0.374 ± j1.621, comment on the expected response. (d) Explain why the plant integrator means P control already gives zero setpoint error, yet integral action may still be wanted. (e) Recommend practical refinements before deployment.
markScheme: From Routh at K = 30: oscillation at ω = √5 rad/s.
Ki = Kp/Ti = 12.8 s⁻¹; Kd = Kp·Td = 6.32 s.
Characteristic: s(s² + 6s + 5)s + Kd s² + Kp s + Ki = s⁴ + 6s³ + (5 + Kd)s² + Kp s + Ki.
Dominant pair ζ = 0.374/1.664 ≈ 0.22: oscillatory, large overshoot (about 62% simulated, as the controller zeros add to it).
Plant is type 1, so P gives zero step error; integral action removes error from constant load disturbances (friction or load torque) entering before the integrator.
Refinements: detune (lower Kp, longer Ti), derivative filter, derivative on measurement, anti-windup, setpoint weighting.
Verifies by simulation or step test against specification.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) For this loop the Routh boundary at K = 30 gives poles at ±j√5, so Pu = 2π/√5 = 2.81 s.

(b) The Ziegler–Nichols rules give Kp = 0.6 × 30 = 18, Ti = Pu/2 = 1.40 s and Td = Pu/8 = 0.351 s. In parallel form, Ki = Kp/Ti = 12.8 s⁻¹ and Kd = Kp·Td = 6.32 s, so C(s) = (6.32s² + 18s + 12.8)/s.

(c) 1 + CP = 0 gives s²(s + 1)(s + 5) + 6.32s² + 18s + 12.81 = 0, which is s⁴ + 6s³ + 11.32s² + 18s + 12.81 = 0. All the roots are in the left half-plane, so the loop is stable. However, the dominant pair −0.374 ± j1.621 has ζ = 0.374/√(0.374² + 1.621²) ≈ 0.22. On its own such a pair would give about 48% overshoot. The controller's two zeros add to the peak, and a step simulation gives about 62%. A strongly oscillatory step response lasting roughly 4/0.374 ≈ 11 s should be expected. This reflects the aggressive quarter-amplitude-decay target.

(d) The plant contains 1/s, so the loop is already type 1 and P or PD control gives zero steady-state error to setpoint steps. However, a constant load torque, such as belt friction or a heavy parcel, enters at the plant input, before that integrator. With P control this leaves a steady speed or position offset of d/Kp. Integral action in the controller removes it, at the cost of phase lag.

(e) Before deployment:
- Detune, for example by halving Kp or lengthening Ti, until the overshoot meets the specification. Check the result by simulation and a careful step test.
- Filter the derivative term, Kd·s/(1 + sTd/N) with N around 10, to limit noise gain.
- Apply derivative action to the measurement rather than the error, to avoid derivative kick on setpoint changes.
- Add anti-windup for motor current or voltage limits, and use setpoint weighting or ramping to soften the setpoint response.

questions.q: An engineer, Kemi, digitises a vibration signal containing components at 1 kHz, 3.5 kHz and 6 kHz using a sampling rate of 8 kHz and a 256-point FFT. (a) State the Nyquist frequency and identify which components alias, and where. (b) Find the FFT bin spacing and the bins in which each component appears. (c) She first tries a first-order RC anti-aliasing filter with fc = 1 kHz. Find its attenuation at 6 kHz and at 3.5 kHz and evaluate the design. (d) For a Butterworth filter with cutoff 3.6 kHz, find the minimum order giving at least 40 dB attenuation at 6 kHz, and the passband droop at 3.5 kHz. (e) Suggest a better system-level approach.
markScheme: 1 kHz and 3.5 kHz are fine; 6 kHz aliases to |6 − 8| = 2 kHz.
RC at 6 kHz: 1/√(1 + 36) = 0.164, which is −15.7 dB.
RC at 3.5 kHz: 1/√(1 + 12.25) = 0.275, which is −11.2 dB; the wanted signal is badly attenuated and the alias only modestly suppressed.
Butterworth: (6/3.6)^(2n) ≥ 10⁴ gives n ≥ 9.02, so n = 10 (n = 9 gives 39.9 dB).
Droop at 3.5 kHz for n = 10: −1.96 dB.
Better approach: oversample (for example 48 kHz or more) with a modest analogue filter, then digital decimation filtering.
Or move the cutoff or sampling rate to widen the transition band.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The Nyquist frequency is fs/2 = 4 kHz. The 1 kHz and 3.5 kHz components are below it and are captured correctly. The 6 kHz component folds to |6 − 8| = 2 kHz, where it masquerades as a genuine 2 kHz vibration.

(b) The bin spacing is Δf = 8000/256 = 31.25 Hz. The components land in these bins:
- 1 kHz: bin 1000/31.25 = 32
- 3.5 kHz: bin 112
- the 6 kHz alias at 2 kHz: bin 64
All fall exactly on bins, so there is no leakage in this idealised case.

(c) For a first-order RC filter, |H| = 1/√(1 + (f/fc)²). At 6 kHz, |H| = 1/√37 = 0.164, which is −15.7 dB. At 3.5 kHz, |H| = 1/√13.25 = 0.275, which is −11.2 dB. The filter cuts the wanted 3.5 kHz component by 11 dB but suppresses the alias by only 16 dB. That is poor for both purposes, because a single pole rolls off at only 20 dB/decade.

(d) A Butterworth filter of order n has |H| = 1/√(1 + (f/fc)^(2n)). For 40 dB at 6 kHz with fc = 3.6 kHz, (6/3.6)^(2n) ≥ 10⁴, so n ≥ 4/(2 log₁₀ 1.667) = 9.02. Order 9 gives 39.9 dB, which just misses, so order 10 is needed. At 3.5 kHz it droops by 10 log₁₀(1 + (3.5/3.6)²⁰) = 1.96 dB. A tenth-order analogue filter is expensive, sensitive to component tolerances, and has poor phase linearity.

(e) The root problem is the narrow transition band between the 3.5 kHz signal and the 4 kHz Nyquist limit. A better design oversamples, at say 48 kHz. A simple second- or third-order analogue filter then easily suppresses anything near 48 kHz that could fold into the band. A sharp digital low-pass filter followed by decimation by 6 brings the rate back to 8 kHz. Digital filters are precise, stable and can have linear phase. Alternatively, a higher final sampling rate such as 16 kHz would relax the analogue requirement directly.

questions.q: A ±1 V square wave at f0 = 1 kHz (odd symmetry) drives a first-order RC low-pass filter whose cutoff is also 1 kHz. (a) Derive or state the Fourier series of the square wave and find the fraction of its power carried by the fundamental and by the first three non-zero harmonics. (b) Find the amplitude and phase of the 1st, 3rd and 5th harmonics at the filter output. (c) Estimate the output power from these harmonics and compare with the input power. (d) Explain the Gibbs phenomenon and whether it would appear in a truncated synthesis of the input and of the output. (e) Lucas claims the output 'is basically a sine wave'. Critically assess this claim quantitatively.
markScheme: Odd, half-wave symmetric, so only odd sine terms: x(t) = (4/π)Σ sin(nω0t)/n for odd n.
Input power = 1 W (normalised); fundamental power = (4/π)²/2 = 0.811, which is 81.1%.
Output power ≈ 0.405 + 0.009 + 0.00125 ≈ 0.416 W, about 42% of the input.
Gibbs: about 9% overshoot of the jump near discontinuities in truncated sums of the input; it persists as terms are added.
The output is continuous (exponential segments), so its series converges uniformly with no Gibbs effect.
Assessment: third harmonic is 0.134/0.900 = 14.9% of the fundamental; fundamental carries about 97% of output power; output is exponential segments with peak 0.917 V, not a sine.
Higher-order filtering or a lower cutoff would be needed for a clean sine.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The square wave is odd and has half-wave symmetry, so only odd sine terms appear: bn = 4/(nπ) for odd n. So x(t) = (4/π)[sin ω0t + (1/3)sin 3ω0t + (1/5)sin 5ω0t + ...]. The input power is 1 W (normalised). The fundamental has amplitude 4/π = 1.273 V and power (4/π)²/2 = 8/π² = 0.811, which is 81.1%. The first three odd harmonics together carry (8/π²)(1 + 1/9 + 1/25) = 0.933, which is 93.3%.

(b) The filter has H(jω) = 1/(1 + jω/ωc) with ωc = ω0. At harmonic n, |H| = 1/√(1 + n²) and ∠H = −arctan n.
- n = 1: 1.273 × 0.707 = 0.900 V, phase −45°
- n = 3: 0.424 × 0.316 = 0.134 V, phase −71.6°
- n = 5: 0.255 × 0.196 = 0.050 V, phase −78.7°

(c) The powers are 0.900²/2 = 0.405, 0.134²/2 = 0.009 and 0.050²/2 = 0.00125, totalling 0.416 W. Higher harmonics add almost nothing, so about 42% of the input power reaches the output.

(d) Near each jump of the input, any truncated Fourier sum overshoots by about 9% of the 2 V jump, about 0.18 V. Adding terms narrows the overshoot but does not reduce its height, because convergence at a discontinuity is not uniform. The filter output is continuous (exponential segments), with coefficients falling as 1/n², so its series converges uniformly with no Gibbs overshoot.

(e) The fundamental carries 0.405/0.416 = 97% of the output power, so in a power sense Lucas has a point. In amplitude terms, though, the third harmonic is 0.134/0.900 = 15% of the fundamental, and the fifth adds another 5.5%. Total harmonic distortion is roughly 16%, which is clearly visible. In the time domain the output is a train of exponential segments peaking at ±0.917 V, with cusps at the switching instants. For a clean sine one would need a lower cutoff (at the cost of amplitude), a higher-order filter, or a resonant band-pass filter at f0.
